item.title: A Confusing Prescription
item.description:
Dreaming

A Confusing Prescription

When dream-medicine can help you reach inside for a real-life cure.

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • If it's goal is to point to the past, the unconscious may choose from memories or associations.
  • Using past memories and current people and situations in dreams can be a way of saying "then and now."
  • The appearance of a "prescription" in a dream may be calling the dreamer to come to a conclusion.
  • Journaling with characters appearing in a dream can often help you tap that similar potential you have inside.

Venus dreamed about receiving a confusing invitation, handwritten on a medicine bottle she couldn't read. When she analyzed the dream, she realized that it invited her to examine her own uncertainty in a moment of transition and seek the cure within herself.

Prescription
Source: Shutterstock/Trygve Finkelsen

The Dream

Venus described the dream in the following way: "I’m wandering around town (London maybe), when I receive a message from Otto about an invite to an Oasis concert. However, it’s handwritten on a medication bottle. The medication bottle is surrounded by COVID stuff. The message is long, with instructions about talking to Jane."

The Conversation

I began by asking, "Do you live in London?"

Venus replied, "I live in California now, but I just came back from London where I have a flat and used to live."

I continued, "How did you feel in this dream?"

Venus said, "I felt a little confused. I was excited by the invite but a bit resentful that I didn't receive it long before the concert date."

I inquired, "What were your thoughts when you saw the long message?"

Venus responded, "I thought it was confusing. Why all this now and why so many instructions?"

Searching for what may have triggered her dream, I asked, "Is there a recent event that has you feeling both confused and excited? Perhaps related to an invitation? You also feel a bit resentful in the dream; has something in your life made you feel resentful?"

Venus connected. "I’m at a crossroads in my life. I'm working in real estate but just graduated in counseling psychology. It's exciting but confusing, because if I want to get licensed, it's a long path. As for an invitation, it feels like anything I receive is always attached to a condition. In the real estate field, any offer I get is attached to a condition. Either the job doesn’t pay enough, or it’s not remote. No vacations, or you must advertise yourself or pay a fee every month. I've put a big effort into this, and I’d like to see results, while I decide how to move forward with the counseling path."

I wondered, "Can you explain what you mean that you used to get invitations?"

Venus responded: "I used to get invitations to concerts and shows, just for who I was. Now everything feels like a scam!"

I asked, "Is that where the invitation to an Oasis concert comes into your dream? Do you like them?"

Venus replied, "Oasis was my favorite band growing up. I was a huge fan, but I don’t like the band anymore."

Moving to another part of her dream, I asked, "What comes to mind about COVID? Did you have it? How did you generally feel around that time?"

Venus explained, "COVID was an important moment for me because I started my degree in transpersonal psychology during that time. I had COVID before it was a thing, so I never really tested positive to it. I felt kind of excited and scared during that time. COVID gave me an opportunity to start again, and not knowing what was coming was scary and exciting. I feel the same way now."

Regarding the note, I wondered, "What were your feelings when you saw this long, handwritten note? It's on a bottle of medicine, and it's surrounded by COVID stuff. Could it be a treatment or cure?"

Venus responded, "The handwritten note was on top of the medication label, and I couldn’t read the instructions. I agree this prescription could represent a treatment or cure. It’s significant that I couldn't read it!"

I noticed a pattern. "We repeat thoughts in our dreams, using different metaphors that point to the same meaning. I wonder if we can tie together some things you've said to make some sense of what you were saying to yourself. For example, London is something that used to be in your life, and the COVID connection is from the past. You say you had COVID 'before it was a thing.' It's the past."

Venus exclaimed, "Yes! Oasis is also from my past! I used to like them, but I don’t anymore."

I concluded, "That's three times you referred to some space you were in that you're moving away from."

Venus agreed. "I'm discussing change. What fits for me now and what doesn't. I'm in transition. I see it. I am no longer at a place where things are getting handed to me."

I added, "You say during the COVID time, you felt kind of excited and scared. Are you harkening back to that feeling now about getting your license?"

Venus said, "That's the confusing part. Getting my license isn’t flexible like the real estate job is. My main question here is if I want to move forward to get licensed as a psychologist or continue in the real estate business."

I offered, "Let's see if we can search out possible solutions inside your dream. For example, tell me about Otto. Who is he and what's he like?"

Venus explained, "Otto is an old friend from London. OMG! There's a fourth example referring to my past! Otto is shy and funny. He doesn’t say much about his job. He's a friend of the singer from Oasis. That’s how we met."

I wondered, "Are you and Otto alike in some ways?"

Venus answered. "Well, I also don’t like to disclose much of what I do because anything I say may be misinterpreted. Being discreet helps me keep things in check. I also think I want to try to stay lighthearted like him."

I continued, "Let's look at Jane, who you're supposed to talk to in your dream. Do you know someone by that name?"

Venus connected. "I had a neighbor named Jane. She's very successful, a high achiever, also unique in her dresses. Her creativity shows inside and outside."

I responded, "The instructions say talk to Jane, but you couldn't read them or the prescription. Maybe this reflects how you are searching for what's next. Do you feel a connection with Jane's qualities?"

Venus considered my question. "Jane is a part of myself I want to engage with. She's a high achiever, and she’s quirky and creative."

I asked, "What could it mean for you to tap into Jane's qualities at this time?"

"Perhaps by dialoguing through writing, I might tap into her energy. I've done this before very successfully. It's a good way of igniting certain qualities I want to bring up in my life."

I agreed. "That process is an ongoing one, especially in life transitions like this one."

What Can We Learn?

It's not unusual to have vivid dreams in moments of transition. The characters in these dreams do not necessarily offer us specific "solutions" for our difficulties, but they often embody characteristics that we can adopt to help us work through the situation.

Tapping into beneficial characteristics is difficult, but dream analysis can help us jumpstart the process. By turning the interior discussion of the dream into an exterior one, analysis brings our unconscious associations into daylight.

In this way we clarify our own ideas, desires, and anxieties. We can receive feedback, and the conscious discussion sharpens our awareness and strategies going forward.

item.title: Why Can the Sex Be So Good in a Bad Relationship?
item.description:
Sex

Why Can the Sex Be So Good in a Bad Relationship?

Research helps explain why great sex and a bad relationship can go together.

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • Sexual satisfaction and relationship satisfaction aren’t the same thing.
  • Sex can provide reassurance and connection when a relationship feels uncertain.
  • Relationship anxiety can increase the emotional importance we attach to sex.
  • Obsessive sexual passion may sometimes make the sex feel even better.

What happens when the sex seems to be telling you one thing about the relationship, while everything else about it is telling you something very different?

Maybe you’ve been there: You’re in a relationship that, for any number of reasons, just isn’t good. Maybe you know, somewhere in the back of your mind, that this relationship probably isn’t going to work.

And yet the sex is incredible. We’re talking about not just good sex, but some of the best sex you’ve ever had.

That experience can be deeply confusing. How can the sex be so good when the relationship itself is so bad?

Surprisingly, researchers haven’t directly examined that question. But research on attachment, sexual motivation, and sexual passion can help us understand how great sex and a bad relationship can coexist.

For starters, how we feel about the sex and how we feel about the relationship aren’t necessarily the same thing. In one study, sexual satisfaction predicted later relationship satisfaction, but relationship satisfaction did not predict later sexual satisfaction. So, the two are related, but they don’t always move together.

We also know that sex can serve purposes beyond physical pleasure. It can provide reassurance, create feelings of closeness, regulate insecurity, and carry different emotional weight, depending on what is happening in the relationship.

Some of those functions may become particularly important when a relationship feels uncertain.

When Sex Is Doing More Than Just Sex

Researchers have examined attachment style and people’s motivations for having sex. People higher in attachment anxiety were particularly likely to report having sex for reasons such as emotional closeness, reassurance, increasing self-esteem, and reducing stress.

Attachment anxiety was also associated with greater sexual passion and with maintaining that passion over time. That may help explain why sex can take on so much importance when a relationship feels uncertain.

If you already feel secure and connected to your partner, sex can be pleasurable, exciting, intimate, and fun. But if you’ve spent the day wondering whether your partner really loves you, whether the relationship is going to survive, or whether the two of you are even okay, sex may also provide a sense of security and connection that’s missing at other times.

And those good feelings don’t necessarily end when sex does. Researchers found that sexual satisfaction remained elevated for about 48 hours after sex, something they called a “sexual afterglow.”

The Emotional Stakes May Be Higher

Research found that people higher in attachment anxiety had more emotionally ambivalent sexual experiences, and their sexual experiences were more strongly related to subsequent interactions with their partners.

Put simply, sex may carry greater emotional and relational weight for people who feel less secure in their relationships.

That doesn’t mean anxious attachment causes great sex, or that everyone having fantastic sex in a troubled relationship is anxiously attached. But it does mean that the same sexual encounter can be simply pleasurable in one relationship and feel enormously consequential in another.

Passion Isn’t One Thing

We tend to assume that intense sexual passion is evidence that something special is happening between two people. But researchers have found that there may be different kinds of sexual passion, with very different implications for relationships.

Researchers distinguish between harmonious sexual passion, which fits comfortably alongside the rest of a person’s life, and obsessive sexual passion, which is more controlling and can involve intrusive sexual thoughts and conflict with other parts of life. Further, research found that harmonious sexual passion strongly predicted both sexual and relationship satisfaction. Another study found that higher obsessive sexual passion among women was associated with greater sexual satisfaction, particularly when their male partners had low levels of inhibited sexual passion.

In other words, feeling intense sexual passion for someone doesn’t necessarily mean the relationship itself is working well. You can really want someone, think about them all the time, and have incredible sexual chemistry with them, even when the relationship outside of sex isn’t good. And sometimes, that obsessive sexual passion may actually make the sex feel even better.

Further, if we believe great sex happens when we find the right person, having incredible sex with someone may make it harder to understand why the rest of the relationship isn’t working. And research tells us some people are more likely to see sexual satisfaction as a matter of finding a naturally compatible partner.

But What About Make-Up Sex?

What about the familiar idea that fighting leads to great make-up sex? The research doesn’t really support it.

One study found that conflict didn’t make couples more likely to have sex that day. In fact, it actually made sex less likely the following day. And when couples did have sex following conflict? They reported lower sexual satisfaction.

So, while make-up sex may be a familiar explanation for why sex can feel so good in a bad relationship, the research suggests that something else may be going on.

So Why Can the Sex Still Be So Good?

To be clear, there isn’t research showing that being in a bad relationship actually makes the sex better.

One possibility is that some sex feels so good, not in spite of the uncertainty in the relationship, but partly because sex temporarily provides the connection and reassurance that may be missing at other times. It doesn’t change whatever isn’t working in the relationship, but it may offer a temporary reprieve from those problems.

And that may help explain how two things that seem like they shouldn’t go together actually can: A relationship can be really bad, while the sex is really, really good.

item.title: How Anti-Gay Propaganda Leads to Real-World Violence
item.description:
Mass Shootings

How Anti-Gay Propaganda Leads to Real-World Violence

Conspiracies and disinformation can radicalize agents of anti-LGBTQ attacks.

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • LGBTQ+ people are 9 times more likely than non-LGBTQ+ people to be victims of a violent hate crime.
  • Data suggests that 70-80% of LGBTQ+ adults have experienced public harassment during their lifetime.
  • "Gay agenda" conspiracies that media commentators and online influencers amplify predict rises in hate crimes.
  • Anti-LGBTQ campaigns predict upticks in bomb threats, vandalism, and violent intimidation.
Source: Leonardo Basso / Unsplash

The “gay agenda” is a disinformation campaign and a set of propagandic conspiracies that are widely adopted by individuals who feel contempt, disgust, fear, or rivalry toward LGBTQ+ folks, often bypassing empathy, critical thinking, and self-reflection in order to defend rhetoric that scapegoats LGBTQ+ people for societal problems they dislike.

Within this constellation of conspiracies are countless accusations of LGBTQ+ people having ulterior motives, or plotting against straight people and traditional values. Examples include speculation that queer people groom children; that queer people manipulate the media to indoctrinate the masses into gayness; and that queer people hate the family and God.

Historically, the idea of a “gay agenda” traces back to Springs of Life Ministries, a California evangelical group that distributed a 1992 video series, "The Gay Agenda," to hundreds of right-wing Christian groups. The video, which claimed “17 percent of homosexuals eat human feces,” sold tens of thousands of copies, and televangelist Pat Robeson broadcast it on "The 700 Club" in 1993.

More alarming than the false alarmism itself is the fact that “gay agenda” propaganda fuels real-world attacks on LGBTQ+ people.

The State of LGBTQ Safety

Anti-LGBTQ+ harassment and violence has remained rampant in recent years. During the Pulse Massacre of 2016, for example, a gunman slaughtered 49 victims and wounded 58 at a gay club in Orlando. In 2022, a gunman preyed upon a gay venue in Colorado Springs, killing five and injuring 25. And as recently as this month, a gunman walked into a gay establishment in Tucson and killed five people.

Dozens of children have also killed themselves after experiencing anti-gay bullying that educators and passive bystanders instigated or did not interrupt. These victims include Asher Brown (age 13, 2010), Seth Walsh (age 13, 2010), Kenneth Weishuhn (age 14, 2012), Jadin Bell (age 15, 2013), Jamel Myles (age 9, 2018), and Nigel Shelby (age 15, 2019), among others.

Source: Joseph Costa / Unsplash

Research on anti-LGBTQ+ bias consistently demonstrates that being perceived as non-heterosexual or gender non-conforming increases the risk of hate crimes and public harassment well into adulthood. According to Pew Research and the Williams Institute at UCLA School of Law, 70 to 80 percent of LGBTQ+ adults have experienced public harassment during their lifetimes. Further, roughly 53 percent of LGBTQ adults report being threatened with physical violence. That rate increases to 40 to 50 percent for transgender people, and is even higher for trans people of color.

Compared to non-LGBTQ+ individuals, LGBTQ+ people are nine times more likely to be victims of a violent hate crime. Annually, the FBI publishes briefs that disaggregate hate crime data by demographic. Their statistics have repeatedly shown that nearly a quarter of all reported hate crimes in the U.S. are motivated by antagonism toward gender and sexual minorities.

What is more, research on perpetrator identity has revealed that heterosexual and cisgender individuals commit nearly 90 percent of bias-motivated, physical assaults on LGBTQ+ people.

Propaganda and Real-World Violence

When I warn about the dangers of “gay agenda” conspiracies, I am not bemoaning mere differences of opinion. That is, I am not talking just about how people think––I’m talking about what they do.

And what anti-LGBTQ+ antagonists and ideologues often do is target LGBTQ+ folks based on “gay agenda” disinformation and propaganda consumed via mass media. In fact, there is a direct link between anti-LGBTQ+ media propaganda and offline hate crimes. Research studies across criminology, social psychology, and media monitoring organizations have explored whether media narratives convert to physical attacks, repeatedly finding statistical correlation between online rhetoric and real-life violence.

For instance, a study by the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) and GLAAD found that half of real-life anti-LGBTQ incidents—hate crimes, street harassment, or vandalism—mirrored anti-LGBTQ+ conspiracies that media commentators and online influencers endorsed and amplified. Sexualizing LGBTQ+ folks as groomers also reduced moral inhibitions to violence.

Source: Mathieu Heurtevin

Relatedly, campaigns against children’s hospitals offering trans-affirming healthcare, as well as educators advocating for LGBTQ-inclusive school climates, correlated with a surge in real-life bomb threats, reactionary protests, vandalism, and violent intimidation toward those institutions and professionals, according to the Center for Countering Digital Hate.

Other researchers found a predictive relationship between online hate speech in certain areas and localized upticks in violence toward those exact groups in those same areas. More specifically, investigations into attacks on LGBTQ+ venues revealed that perpetrators were radicalized by anti-LGBTQ+ disinformation prior to committing mass violence.

Those who rationalize, minimize, or altogether deny anti-LGBTQ violence may absolve their guilt by pretending the anti-LGBTQ+ propaganda consumed and circulated online is compartmentalized from real life. Yet ample evidence proves that anti-LGBTQ+ hate crime perpetrators are more likely to act after witnessing media propagandists amplifying hostile rhetorical signals, which they interpret both as proof that their biases are broadly shared and as social permission to assault or murder LGBTQ+ people.

I hope all anti-LGBTQ+ people fighting an imaginary "gay agenda" feel the moral weight of their complicity, that they realize discomfort with new or unfamiliar terrain does not automatically substantiate an actual threat, and that they understand reckless contrarianism doesn't make them virtuous or a true "free thinker."

item.title: Can Post-Traumatic Growth Help Protect Against Suicide?
item.description:
Suicide

Can Post-Traumatic Growth Help Protect Against Suicide?

How connection, regulation, and hope may create a pathway away from crisis.

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • Suicide risk can involve experiences of disconnection, overwhelming distress, and loss of hope.
  • Research suggests post-traumatic growth (PTG) is associated with lower levels of suicidal ideation.
  • A shift can begin with small movements toward 3 aspects of the PTG process: connection, regulation, and hope.

The night before Kevin Hines jumped from the Golden Gate Bridge, he wanted someone to ask if he was thinking about harming himself. He was.

Kevin describes that night, and the day he jumped, in painstaking detail in his book Cracked, Not Broken. What is striking about Kevin's story is how often he describes longing for human connection while simultaneously feeling unable to reach for it.

As he rode the city bus to the Golden Gate Bridge with the intention of ending his life, he wished someone would say something to him. If anyone communicated that they cared, that he mattered, that he wasn't a burden, he resolved that he would not jump that day. But nobody did. Kevin describes tears streaming uncontrollably down his face as he rode that bus. His story raises an uncomfortable question: What might have happened if someone had noticed how he was doing?

There is another striking feature of Kevin's story: the profound dysregulation he was experiencing. He wasn't sleeping. He was in psychosis. He was experiencing overwhelming psychological pain and could not find a way to interrupt or reduce it.

His story points to something else: When we are overwhelmed, our ability to access coping strategies and choose something that might help us feel differently can become severely constrained. Even a small amount of relief or connection can open up new possibility for someone who is profoundly dysregulated.

And there is one other powerful aspect of Kevin’s experience worth noting: the loss of hope. In Kevin’s account of that night, he could not see a future that felt meaningfully different from the present. No clear way existed to solve the problems that had brought him to such profound pain.

So Kevin jumped.

I won't tell you the rest of his story in case you want to read his incredible book for yourself. What is important for you to know is that Kevin lived to tell about it.

Learning from Kevin and from Psychological Theory

Most theories of suicide point toward similar human experiences of struggle—the ones we see in Kevin’s story:

  • Disconnection: Feeling alone, feeling that you don't belong, or feeling that you are a burden.
  • Dysregulation: Being overwhelmed by psychological pain and feeling unable to tolerate what you are experiencing.
  • Loss of hope: Being unable to see a future that is meaningfully different from the present.

These experiences can interact and reinforce one another. Disconnection can deepen distress. Dysregulation can make it harder to reach for other people or access resources that might help. And when we cannot imagine a different future, it can become increasingly difficult to tolerate the present.

This raises an important question for suicide prevention: If disconnection, dysregulation, and hopelessness can be part of the pathway toward crisis, could movement in the other direction—toward connection, regulation, and hope—help create a pathway away from crisis?

Kevin's story gives us one way to think about that question. After his attempt, his story includes psychiatric hospitalizations, medication, difficult periods, setbacks, and the ongoing work of managing his mental health. But it also includes people.

Kevin’s connection with his father was renewed when he saw the tears his father shed at the possibility of losing him. His uncle came to his bedside daily, bringing books that eventually helped Kevin reconnect with a sense of purpose. With support, Kevin developed practices that helped him manage his symptoms and stay on a path toward living.

His story does not suggest that continuing on is simple or linear. It does, however, offer a glimpse of what movement in the other direction can look like.

Where Posttraumatic Growth Enters the Conversation

Research has begun to suggest an association between post-traumatic growth (PTG) and lower levels of suicidal ideation and behavior (Bush et al., 2011; Yasdiman et al., 2022a; Yasdiman et al., 2022b; Jeong, 2025). In our work, we often ask ourselves: Why might PTG be related to suicidality in this way? Could processes involved in PTG, such as connection, regulation, and hope, play a role in helping people move away from suicidal ideation?

  • Connection: Connection is at the heart of the PTG process. At its core PTG involves “Expert Companionship”, the idea that companions are critical to navigating hard times. When people walk by our side through darkness, we see that we aren’t alone in our struggles.
  • Regulation: Regulation is also part of the PTG process. When people struggle to make sense of hard times, they often search for ways to manage the emotional distress that comes with them. As we find ways to get through difficult moments, we begin to develop a sense that we can tolerate difficult emotions without being completely consumed by them. We can get through this moment. Then the next one.
  • Hope: In the process of PTG people are driven to understand what has happened and to find meaning in the aftermath of experiences they never would have chosen. Sometimes that meaning involves reconnecting with purpose. Sometimes it involves recognizing what matters most. When we reconnect with what matters to us, we reconnect with the possibility that something meaningful is still ahead, and that instills hope.

A New Beginning

Kevin Hines’ story gives us a deeply human example of what these ideas can look like in one person's life. It also invites us to ask important questions, such as:

  • When people experience profound struggle, what helps them reconnect with other people?
  • What helps them regain enough regulation to tolerate the next difficult moment?
  • What helps them begin to imagine a future worth living?

Perhaps one of the most useful things PTG can offer is a framework for understanding how, through struggle and with the support of others, we may begin to find a way forward.

If you or someone you know is struggling with thoughts of suicide, you can reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988, or the Crisis Text Line by texting HOME to 741741.

To learn more about post-traumatic growth and expert companionship, visit Boulder Crest Foundation.
